justification: Target query: "how to calculate time complexity" (CONTENT_PLAN.md §7.1 row 2). I fetched four of the pages that currently rank for this query and adjacent phrasing (GeeksforGeeks's loop-analysis page, its general time/space-complexity page, its 'analysis of loops' page, and freeCodeCamp's introductory piece). All four stop at single/nested-loop Big-O and simple recursion; none covers dependent-bound (triangular) loops with a derived closed form, recursion trees, recurrence relations, the Master Theorem (any of its three cases), the regularity condition, or when the theorem doesn't apply (subtractive recurrences, unequal subproblems, the case-2/3 gap). This article covers all of that, each claim backed by an instrumented C# program whose measured counts match the derived closed form, plus a genuinely reusable five-step procedure at the end (not a rehash of headings). That is a real, verified content gap the top results leave open, matching the plan's stated angle ('a procedure a reader can apply, with 8 graded code fragments analysed fully'). Structurally the article earns its assigned Q (question-driven) shape: every heading is a real search-style question, distinct from the prerequisite big-o-notation.md's declarative headings, and it explicitly avoids re-teaching big-o-notation's five rules of thumb, instead measuring and extending each one. Boundaries with the three other planned complexity/algorithms siblings are documented and sensible in docs/crosslinks/complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion.md, so the missing body links to /algorithms/recursion/, /complexity/space-complexity/ and /complexity/best-average-worst-case/ are not held against it; the one live cross-link used (/algorithms/binary-search/) resolves to a published (draft:false) article, and the two anchor links into big-o-notation.md point at headings that actually exist there. No filler intro/outro, no keyword stuffing, no boilerplate 'Introduction/Conclusion' headings, exercises vary in form (find-the-trap, extend-the-code, apply-it, measure-it) and none leaks its output panel above the solution. I checked whether the article states its toolchain wherever it reports measured numbers (the pilot-round rule flagged on a sibling article this batch): every 'measured' figure here is a deterministic step/call/comparison count from `long` counters (steps, calls, matches, moves, compares), not a wall-clock timing, so there is no hardware- or runtime-dependent number that needs a 'ran on .NET X on OS Y/CPU Z' disclosure — unlike big-o-notation.md, this article never times anything with Stopwatch, and it correctly has no such statement. The score is held below the top of the range by a real sourcing-hygiene problem: 'Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed., chapter 7 (Quicksort)' is listed in front matter but never cited anywhere in the body (the quicksort-worst-case paragraph cites only NIST's 'hard split, easy merge' page), which the binding pilot-round lesson calls out by name as a finding, and which reads as an unused, decorative citation rather than a source the text actually leans on. Two smaller citation-weave gaps compound this (see issues). None of these are fabrications or factual errors — I independently fetched the NIST DADS 'easy split, hard merge' entry and the Microsoft Learn Thread constructor page and confirmed the article's own phrasing is original (not paraphrased from either) and that the '1 megabyte' default stack-size claim is accurate per that page — but they are real, fixable sourcing gaps that keep this from the very top of the scale.
